+    let source = source_text(db, file);
+    if !module_name_changes.may_affect_source(&source) {
+        return Vec::new();
+    }
+
+    let parsed_module = ruff_db::parsed::parsed_module(db, program_file.python_file(db)).load(db);
+    let root = AnyNodeRef::from(parsed_module.syntax());
+    let model = SemanticModel::new(db, program_file);
+    let mut bound_name_change_cache = BoundNameChangeCache::new(module_name_changes);
+
+    let import_statement_changes = {
+        let mut import_statement_visitor =
+            ImportStatementVisitor::new(db, &model, &mut bound_name_change_cache);
+        root.visit_source_order(&mut import_statement_visitor);
+        import_statement_visitor.changes
+    };
+
+    let mut module_reference_visitor = ModuleReferenceVisitor::new(
+        db,
+        &model,
+        &source,
+        &import_statement_changes.bound_name_changes,
+        &mut bound_name_change_cache,
+    );
+    root.visit_source_order(&mut module_reference_visitor);
+
+    let mut edits = import_statement_changes.edits;
+    edits.extend(module_reference_visitor.edits);
+    edits
+}
+
+/// Computes imported name and module name edits, and records bound name changes.
+///
+/// For example, renaming `pkg.old` to `pkg.new` changes
+///
+/// ```python
+/// import pkg.old
+/// ```
+///
+/// to
+///
+/// ```python
+/// import pkg.new
+/// ```
+///
+/// and
+///
+/// ```python
+/// from pkg.old import C
+/// ```
+///
+/// to
+///
+/// ```python
+/// from pkg.new import C
+/// ```
+///
+/// For the moment, the computed edits never change the form of an import statement. For instance,
+/// we never introduce an explicit alias where there wasn't one before, or change the import level in
+/// a relative import.
+///
+/// The visitor uses a [`ModuleMemberNameAnalyzer`] to follow bound name changes through re-exports,
+/// sharing a [`BoundNameChangeCache`] across import statements.
+struct ImportStatementVisitor<'a, 'db> {
+    db: &'db dyn Db,
+    editor: ImportStatementEditor<'a, 'db>,
+    bound_name_change_cache: &'a mut BoundNameChangeCache<'db>,
+    changes: ImportStatementChanges<'db>,
+}
+
+impl<'a, 'db> ImportStatementVisitor<'a, 'db> {
+    fn new(
+        db: &'db dyn Db,
+        model: &'a SemanticModel<'db>,
+        bound_name_change_cache: &'a mut BoundNameChangeCache<'db>,
+    ) -> Self {
+        Self {
+            db,
+            editor: ImportStatementEditor::new(model, bound_name_change_cache.module_name_changes),
+            bound_name_change_cache,
+            changes: ImportStatementChanges::default(),
+        }
+    }
+}
+
+impl<'a> SourceOrderVisitor<'a> for ImportStatementVisitor<'a, '_> {
+    fn enter_node(&mut self, node: AnyNodeRef<'a>) -> TraversalSignal {
+        let changes = match node {
+            AnyNodeRef::StmtImport(statement) => self.editor.edit_plain_import(statement),
+            AnyNodeRef::StmtImportFrom(statement) => self.editor.edit_import_from(
+                statement,
+                &mut ModuleMemberNameAnalyzer::new(self.db, self.bound_name_change_cache),
+            ),
+            _ => return TraversalSignal::Traverse,
+        };
+
+        if let Some(changes) = changes {
+            self.changes.extend(changes);
+        }
+
+        // The import statement has been handled, so its descendants
+        // (e.g., aliases) do not need a separate visit.
+        TraversalSignal::Skip
+    }
+
+    // Plain import statements and import-from statements cannot occur inside expressions.
+    fn visit_expr(&mut self, _expr: &'a ast::Expr) {}
+}
+
+/// Computes edits and bound name changes for one import statement.
+struct ImportStatementEditor<'a, 'db> {
+    model: &'a SemanticModel<'db>,
+    module_name_changes: &'a ModuleNameChanges<'db>,
+}
+
+impl<'a, 'db> ImportStatementEditor<'a, 'db> {
+    fn new(model: &'a SemanticModel<'db>, module_name_changes: &'a ModuleNameChanges<'db>) -> Self {
+        Self {
+            model,
+            module_name_changes,
+        }
+    }
+
+    /// Computes imported name edits for a plain import statement, such as `import old` to `import new`.
+    ///
+    /// Returns `None` if no source edits or bound name changes are produced.
+    fn edit_plain_import(
+        &self,
+        statement: &ast::StmtImport,
+    ) -> Option<ImportStatementChanges<'db>> {
+        let mut changes = ImportStatementChanges::default();
+        for alias in &statement.names {
+            match self.should_edit_imported_name_for_plain_import(alias) {
+                EditDecision::Yes(new_imported_name) => {
+                    self.record_imported_name_edit(&mut changes, alias, new_imported_name);
+                }
+                EditDecision::No => continue,
+                EditDecision::Omit => return None,
+            }
+        }
+
+        (!changes.is_empty()).then_some(changes)
+    }
+
+    /// Computes imported name and module name edits for an import-from statement.
+    ///
+    /// For example, `from pkg import old` becomes `from pkg import new`, and
+    /// `from pkg.old import C` becomes `from pkg.new import C`.
+    ///
+    /// Returns `None` when the module cannot be resolved or the rename produces no source edits
+    /// or bound name changes.
+    fn edit_import_from(
+        &self,
+        statement: &ast::StmtImportFrom,
+        module_member_name_analyzer: &mut ModuleMemberNameAnalyzer<'_, 'db>,
+    ) -> Option<ImportStatementChanges<'db>> {
+        let resolved_module = self.model.resolve_module(
+            statement.module.as_ref().map(ast::Identifier::as_str),
+            statement.level,
+        )?;
+        let import_from_module_edit = if let Some(new_module_name) = self
+            .module_name_changes
+            .new_module_name(resolved_module.name(self.model.db()))
+        {
+            let module = statement.module.as_ref()?;
+            Some(self.import_from_module_edit(module, new_module_name))
+        } else {
+            None
+        };
+
+        let mut changes = ImportStatementChanges::default();
+        for alias in &statement.names {
+            match self.should_edit_imported_name_for_import_from(
+                alias,
+                resolved_module,
+                module_member_name_analyzer,
+            ) {
+                EditDecision::Yes(new_imported_name) => {
+                    self.record_imported_name_edit(&mut changes, alias, new_imported_name);
+                }
+                EditDecision::No | EditDecision::Omit => continue,
+            }
+        }
+
+        // An import-from statement may still have a module name edit when no imported names change.
+        if let Some(import_from_module_edit) = import_from_module_edit {
+            changes.edits.push(import_from_module_edit);
+        }
+
+        (!changes.is_empty()).then_some(changes)
+    }
+
+    /// Chooses an imported name edit for a plain import statement (e.g., `pkg.old` to `pkg.new`
+    /// in the statement `import pkg.old`).
+    fn should_edit_imported_name_for_plain_import(&self, alias: &ast::Alias) -> EditDecision {
+        let Some(resolved_module) = self.model.resolve_module(Some(alias.name.as_str()), 0) else {
+            return EditDecision::No;
+        };
+
+        let Some(new_module_name) = self
+            .module_name_changes
+            .new_module_name(resolved_module.name(self.model.db()))
+        else {
+            return EditDecision::No;
+        };
+
+        EditDecision::replace_if_changed(alias.name.as_str(), new_module_name.as_str())
+    }
+
+    /// Chooses an imported name edit for an import-from statement, including re-exports.
+    ///
+    /// For example, renaming `pkg.old` can change the imported name `old` in both
+    /// `from pkg import old` and `from facade import old` when `facade` re-exports `old`.
+    fn should_edit_imported_name_for_import_from(
+        &self,
+        alias: &ast::Alias,
+        resolved_module: Module<'db>,
+        module_member_name_analyzer: &mut ModuleMemberNameAnalyzer<'_, 'db>,
+    ) -> EditDecision {
+        if !self
+            .module_name_changes
+            .is_old_module_basename(alias.name.as_str())
+        {
+            return EditDecision::No;
+        }
+
+        if let Some(imported_module) = self.directly_imported_submodule(alias, resolved_module) {
+            let Some(new_module_name) = self
+                .module_name_changes
+                .new_module_name(imported_module.name(self.model.db()))
+            else {
+                return EditDecision::No;
+            };
+
+            return EditDecision::replace_if_changed(
+                alias.name.as_str(),
+                new_module_name.last_component(),
+            );
+        }
+
+        module_member_name_analyzer.should_edit_module_member(
+            self.model,
+            resolved_module,
+            alias.name.as_str(),
+        )
+    }
+
+    /// Constructs a module name edit, preserving its prefix and the import level.
+    ///
+    /// The module parent is unchanged, so only the final component needs replacing.
+    /// For example, `from ..pkg.old import C` becomes `from ..pkg.new import C`.
+    fn import_from_module_edit(
+        &self,
+        module: &ast::Identifier,
+        new_module_name: &ModuleName,
+    ) -> FileRenameEdit {
+        let replacement = if let Some((prefix, _)) = module.as_str().rsplit_once('.') {
+            format!("{prefix}.{}", new_module_name.last_component())
+        } else {
+            new_module_name.last_component().to_string()
+        };
+        self.source_edit(module.range, replacement)
+    }
+
+    /// Identifies an imported name that resolves to a direct submodule.
+    ///
+    /// For example, `old` in `from pkg import old` when it resolves to `pkg/old.py`.
+    fn directly_imported_submodule(
+        &self,
+        alias: &ast::Alias,
+        resolved_module: Module<'db>,
+    ) -> Option<Module<'db>> {
+        let db = self.model.db();
+        let module_name = resolved_module.name(db);
+        let imported_module = resolved_module_from_type(self.model, alias)?;
+        let imported_module_name = imported_module.name(db);
+
+        if alias.name.as_str() != imported_module_name.last_component()
+            || imported_module_name.parent().as_ref() != Some(module_name)
+        {
+            return None;
+        }
+
+        // Without a package definition for `old`, `from pkg import old` imports `pkg.old`
+        // directly (for example, when `pkg/__init__.py` is empty).
+        if self
+            .model
+            .definitions_for_module_global(resolved_module, alias.name.as_str())
+            .is_none()
+        {
+            return Some(imported_module);
+        }
+
+        // In `pkg/__init__.py`, `from . import old` imports `pkg.old` directly and defines
+        // the package's `old` bound name. Resolving that name as a re-export would analyze
+        // the same import again.
+        if file_to_module(db, self.model.program_file().resolver_file(db))
+            .is_some_and(|importing_module| importing_module.name(db) == module_name)
+        {
+            return Some(imported_module);
+        }
+
+        None
+    }
+
+    /// Records an imported name edit and any resulting bound name change.
+    ///
+    /// For example, renaming `pkg/old.py` to `pkg/new.py` changes the imported name `pkg.old` in
+    /// `import pkg.old` to `pkg.new`, but keeps the bound name `pkg`. Conversely, the same rename
+    /// changes the imported name `old` in `from pkg import old` to `new` and also changes the bound
+    /// name.
+    fn record_imported_name_edit(
+        &self,
+        changes: &mut ImportStatementChanges<'db>,
+        alias: &ast::Alias,
+        new_imported_name: String,
+    ) {
+        if let Some(new_bound_name) = Self::bound_name_replacement(alias, &new_imported_name) {
+            let definition =
+                ty_python_core::semantic_index(self.model.db(), self.model.program_file())
+                    .expect_single_definition(alias);
+            changes
+                .bound_name_changes
+                .insert(definition, new_bound_name.to_owned());
+        }
+
+        changes
+            .edits
+            .push(self.source_edit(alias.name.range, new_imported_name));
+    }
+
+    /// Constructs a source edit, such as replacing the imported name `old` with `new`.
+    fn source_edit(&self, range: TextRange, replacement: String) -> FileRenameEdit {
+        RangedValue {
+            range: FileRange::new(self.model.file(), range),
+            value: replacement,
+        }
+    }
+
+    /// Returns the new bound name if changing the imported name also changes its binding.
+    fn bound_name_replacement<'name>(
+        alias: &ast::Alias,
+        new_imported_name: &'name str,
+    ) -> Option<&'name str> {
+        if alias.asname.is_some() {
+            return None;
+        }
+
+        // `import pkg.old` binds `pkg`, while `from pkg import old` binds `old`.
+        // The first component of the imported name gives the bound name in both cases.
+        let old_bound_name = Self::first_component(alias.name.as_str());
+        let new_bound_name = Self::first_component(new_imported_name);
+        (old_bound_name != new_bound_name).then_some(new_bound_name)
+    }
+
+    /// Retrieves the first component of an imported name: `pkg` for `pkg.old`, or `old` for `old`.
+    fn first_component(alias_name: &str) -> &str {
+        alias_name
+            .split_once('.')
+            .map(|(first, _)| first)
+            .unwrap_or(alias_name)
+    }
+}
+
+type BoundNameChanges<'db> = FxHashMap<Definition<'db>, String>;
+
+#[derive(Default)]
+struct ImportStatementChanges<'db> {
+    /// Source edits to imported names and module names.
+    edits: Vec<FileRenameEdit>,
+    /// Maps import definitions to new bound names for reference edits.
+    bound_name_changes: BoundNameChanges<'db>,
+}
+
+impl ImportStatementChanges<'_> {
+    fn is_empty(&self) -> bool {
+        self.edits.is_empty() && self.bound_name_changes.is_empty()
+    }
+
+    fn extend(&mut self, other: Self) {
+        self.edits.extend(other.edits);
+        self.bound_name_changes.extend(other.bound_name_changes);
+    }
+}
+
+/// Caches bound name decisions by import definition while computing edits for one file.
+struct BoundNameChangeCache<'db> {
+    module_name_changes: &'db ModuleNameChanges<'db>,

`Self` can be both the owner’s argument and the return type of the method being projected. Protocol receiver binding still replaces both occurrences with the receiver type.

```python
from __future__ import annotations
from typing import Protocol, Self, reveal_type

class P[C](Protocol):
    def method(self, value: C) -> tuple[C, Self]:
        def check(other: P[Self], v: Self):
            reveal_type(other.method(v))
        raise NotImplementedError
```

Both the base and this PR reject `v`, expecting `P[Self]`, and reveal `tuple[P[Self], P[Self]]`. Changing `class P[C](Protocol)` to `class P[C]` on this PR gives the expected `tuple[Self, P[Self]]` and accepts the call. Could protocol receiver binding preserve the enclosing `Self` in the same way?

An alias around the owner’s argument still allows the method to capture `T`.

```python
from typing import reveal_type

type Items[A] = list[A]

class Box[C]:
    @staticmethod
    def get[T](value: T) -> C:
        def check(other: Box[Items[T]], number: int):
            result = other.get(number)
            reveal_type(result)
            wrong: list[int] = result
        raise NotImplementedError
```

Both the base and this PR reveal `list[int]` and accept the assignment. The result should be `list[T]`, with `T` fixed by `other`. A local `type Items = list[T]` inside `get` has the same problem when the receiver is `Box[Items]`. Could the collision and freshness searches account for both explicit alias arguments and variables captured by the alias body?

The direct method call now preserves the enclosing `T`, but saving the same bound method on the instance still loses it.

```python
from __future__ import annotations
from typing import reveal_type

class Box[C]:
    def __init__(self):
        self.callback = self.method

    def method[T](self, x: T) -> tuple[C, T]:
        def check(other: Box[T], arg: int):
            reveal_type(other.callback(arg))
            reveal_type(other.method(arg))
        raise NotImplementedError
```

Both the base and this PR reveal `tuple[int, int]` for `other.callback(arg)`. On this PR `other.method(arg)` correctly gives `tuple[T@method, int]`. `ClassType::own_instance_member` applies the owner specialization directly. Could we share this freshening step with that lookup path?

I think "declaration's type", as a phrase, suffers from precisely the ambiguity that this comment aims to clarify. "the type declared by this declaration" might be clearer, though it sounds a bit redundant.

I _think_ what this is trying to say is that our expression-types map implicitly stores a "denoted type" for an expression in annotation position that we infer as a type expression, but stores a "runtime-inhabited type" for expressions in value position, and this distinction is entirely implicit and contextual, which is error-prone. That does seem like a useful note, and even arguably worth a TODO, since it can cause bugs. (I have a draft PR attempting to clarify/split this better in the representation, but it's hard to do without memory regressions.)

I think the current comment doesn't communicate this very clearly. It took me a while to understand what "Annotation expressions are inputs to declaration inference" even means or why it's relevant here.
Similar note as in the other added doc comments on this topic. I think I understand what this is getting at, but I think the explanation could be a lot clearer, and an example would help.

With `suffix: tuple[bool, str] = (True, "ok")` inside `bounded`, the same `reveal_type(bounded(1, *suffix))` gives `tuple[Literal[True], Literal["ok"]]` on main and `tuple[Literal[True]]` on this branch. @@ -0,0 +1,2057 @@
+//! Computes source edits for Python file renames.
+//!
+//! ## Overview
+//!
+//! [`will_rename_files`] maps filesystem renames to module names, then computes edits for import
+//! statements and references in indexed project files. It does not move files, discover package
+//! contents, validate the filesystem operation, or normalize the returned edits.
+//!
+//! EXAMPLE:
+//!
+//! When `pkg/old.py` is renamed to `pkg/new.py`, the following code:
+//!
+//! ```python
+//! from pkg import old
+//! print(old.C)
+//! ```
+//!
+//! is updated like so:
+//!
+//! ```python
+//! from pkg import new
+//! print(new.C)
+//! ```
+//!
+//! [`will_rename_files`] computes edits over all files in parallel using [`edits_for_file`]. That
+//! in turn computes edits for a single file in two distinct AST passes: [`ImportStatementVisitor`]
+//! visits import statements and computes edits for them, then [`ModuleReferenceVisitor`] visits
+//! all references to imported modules and computes edits for those references. Those two sets of
+//! edits are combined to produce the final result.
+//!
+//! ## Terminology
+//!
+//! Below is the anatomy of the two types of import statement.
+//!
+//! A "plain" import statement:
+//!
+//! ```text
+//!              Alias
+//!        +---------------+
+//! import pkg.old as stable
+//!        |          |
+//!        |          explicit alias
+//!        imported name
+//! ```
+//!
+//! and an "import-from" statement:
+//!
+//! ```text
+//!                       Alias
+//!                   +-----------+
+//! from ..pkg import old as stable
+//!      | |            |      |
+//!      | module name  |      explicit alias
+//!      |              imported name
+//!      |
+//!      import level
+//! ```
+//!
+//! From there, we can layer on a few additional terms.
+//!

+//! print(new.C)
+//! ```

+//! in turn computes edits for a single file in two distinct AST passes: [`ImportStatementVisitor`]

+//! ## Terminology

+//! Below is the anatomy of the two types of import statement.

+//! A "plain" import statement:

+//!        |          explicit alias

+//! ```
+//!

+//!                       Alias

+//!      |              imported name

+//! | Module reference | The use of a module in an expression. | `old` in `old.C`; `pkg.old` in `pkg.old.C`. |

+//! | Imported name edit | Replacement of an imported name. | `import old` → `import new`, `import pkg.old` → `import pkg.new` |
+//! | Module name edit | Replacement of the module name in an import-from statement. | `from old import C` → `from new import C`. |
+//! | Bound name change | Change to a bound name caused by an imported name edit. | `old` → `new`; no bound name change for an explicit alias like `as stable`. |

+/// Computes source edits for a batch of Python file renames.
+///
+/// The following types of rename request are not yet supported:
+///
+/// - A request that renames a directory
+/// - A request that changes a module parent (e.g., renaming `a.old` to `b.new` or `new`)
+/// - A request that renames an `__init__.py` or `__init__.pyi` file
+/// - A request that changes the extension of a module (e.g., from `.py` to `.pyi`)
+///
+/// When a rename batch contains both supported and unsupported requests, the unsupported requests
+/// are skipped while the supported ones produce edits as normal.
+///
+/// The returned edits refer to the original files and source ranges. The caller must sort the edits
+/// and handle duplicates and overlaps before applying them.
+///
+/// ## Unsupported edits
+///
+/// Even for supported renames, some occurrences are not updated:
+///
+/// - Name references supplied by star imports, such as `from pkg import *`.
+/// - Names in `global` and `nonlocal` declarations, and references whose resolution crosses those
+///   declarations.
+/// - Names and attributes being assigned to or deleted. Receiver expressions can still be updated.
+/// - Names in ordinary strings, including `__all__` entries and dynamic imports (although module
+///   references in string annotations are supported).
+///
+/// Other edits may still be returned, so an import can be updated while a reference to its old
+/// name remains unchanged.
+///
+/// Additionally, an ambiguous imported name is left unchanged even when other names in the same
+/// import-from statement are updated. For example, suppose we rename `old.py` to `new.py` and
+/// `other.py` to `another.py`:
+///
+/// ```python
+/// # facade.py
+/// import old
+/// import other
+/// if flag:
+///     old = 0
+///
+/// # use.py
+/// from facade import other, old
+/// ```
+///
+/// In the import from `facade`, `old` may or may not refer to the renamed module, so it is left
+/// unchanged. The import becomes `from facade import another, old`.
+fn will_rename_files(db: &dyn Db, renames: &[FileRename]) -> Vec<FileRenameEdit> {
+    let files: Vec<_> = db.project().files(db).iter().collect();
+    let module_name_changes = ModuleNameChanges::new(db, renames);
+    if module_name_changes.is_empty() {
+        return Vec::new();
+    }
+
+    files
+        .into_par_iter()
+        .map_with_db(db, |db, file| {
+            edits_for_file(db, file, &module_name_changes)
+        })
+        .flatten()
+        .collect()
+}

+    /// The source file before the rename.
+    file: File,
+    /// The destination path, which need not exist yet.
+    new_path: SystemPathBuf,
+}
+
+/// A replacement and the file range containing it.
+type FileRenameEdit = RangedValue<String>;

+/// Maps old module names to new module names for supported file renames.

+    // A map from old module name to new module name for supported rename operations.
+    module_renames: FxHashMap<&'db ModuleName, ModuleName>,
+    // The module basename for each key in `module_renames` (e.g., `old` in `pkg.old`).

I haven't looked at the code yet, I've only been reading the docs. What I understand the responsibility of those two visitors are:

1. `ImportStatementVisitor`: Searches for import statements that need to be rewritten and it collects the local definitions that need to be renamed as part of it
2. `ModuleReferenceVisitor`: Rename the local references


When I asked codex about it, it included an example. I found that quiet useful:

--- 

ImportStatementVisitor computes edits to import statements and records which local definitions consequently change their bound name. For example, from pkg import old → from pkg import new records the import definition’s old → new change. An explicit alias preserves the bound name, so it produces no such mapping.

ModuleReferenceVisitor updates references to those definitions, using reaching definitions to distinguish them from unrelated bindings with the same spelling.

---

It might also be helpful to explain why two passes are necessary (because function bodies can reference import statements that come later within the same file).

Can we drop this branch and the new `Type::resolve_typevars` helper? Only regular callables reach `Binding::freshen_bound_typevars`, and their `constructor_context` is `None`. Keeping the alias here exposes a difference between an alias and its expansion during call inference:

```python
type Items[T] = list[T]

def copy[T](items: Items[T], v: T) -> None:
    copy([1], "a")
```

Main accepts this recursive call. On this branch we infer `list[int]` for the literal and reject it after `"a"` widens `T`. Spelling the parameter as `list[T]` still works on both revisions. This also affects an ordinary call to an inherited method. If `A` and `B` inherit the same generic `copy` method and `x: A | B`, the base accepts `x.copy([1], "a")` and this version rejects it.

Could `inferable_typevar_occurrences` visit the alias’s stored arguments? That would let inference revisit the list literal once it has seen the second argument.

Keeping the starred annotation also changes how we infer argument types from the expected return type:

```python
from typing import TypedDict

class Item(TypedDict):
    value: int

def collect[*Ts](*args: *tuple[*Ts]) -> tuple[*Ts]:
    x: tuple[Item] = collect({"value": 1})
    raise NotImplementedError
```

Main uses `Item` as the context for the dictionary literal on the recursive call. On this branch we infer `tuple[dict[str, int]]` and report an assignment error. The same loss of context affects a nonrecursive call. Outside `collect`, set `f = partial(collect) if flag else collect` using `functools.partial`. The base accepts `x: tuple[Item] = f({"value": 1})`, while this version infers `tuple[Item] | tuple[dict[str, int]]`.

`typevartuple_argument_context` only recognizes a bare pack. Could we teach it to find the pack in the preserved tuple annotation and account for any fixed prefix or suffix when matching arguments?

Could we keep expanding fixed-length starred tuple annotations here? There’s no pack to preserve in `*tuple[int, str]`. This also affects ordinary calls through an inherited method:

```python
class Base:
    def run[T](self, value: T, *args: *tuple[int, str]) -> None: ...

class A(Base): ...
class B(Base): ...

def check(x: A | B, ints: list[int]) -> None:
    x.run(0, *ints)
```

Main reports that the second position requires a `str` and the list supplies an `int`. This PR accepts the call. The two bound methods share a generic context, so call binding freshens the signature even though `check` is nonrecursive. Expanding fixed tuples would preserve the positional check while still letting us keep the boundaries around an unsolved `TypeVarTuple`.

This drops a solved type variable even when `__new__` uses it in a different position in the return type. For example:

```python
from __future__ import annotations

class C[T, U]:
    first: T

    def __new__(cls, x: T, y: U) -> C[U, T]:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def f(self, x: int, y: str) -> int:
        return C(x, y).first
```

Main infers `C[str, int]` inside `f` and correctly reports that we're returning a `str`. On this branch we infer `C[int, str]` and accept the return. We get the class arguments from the already-specialized `C[U, T]`, then substitute them into `C[U, T]` again, undoing the swap. Main already gets the call wrong outside the class, but this loses the correct result inside the class too.

Could we keep the variables solved by `__new__` and use the downstream constructor to fill only the ones left unsolved?
I also don't think we'll need these tests if we just ignore any method with a decorator.

+```toml

+lint.select = ["PLE0211"]

+## Instance and class methods
+
+A bound method receives an instance or class as an implicit positional argument.
+
+```py
+class Example:
+    def method():  # snapshot: no-method-argument
+        return 1
+
+    @classmethod
+    def class_method():  # error: [no-method-argument]
+        return 1

+        return 1

+ --> src/mdtest_snippet.py:2:9
+  |
+2 |     def method():  # snapshot: no-method-argument
+  |         ^^^^^^
+```
+
+## Functions and methods that accept a receiver
+
+Static methods and functions outside a class do not receive an implicit argument.
+A positional parameter or `*args` can receive the implicit argument of a method.
+
+```py
+def function():  # no diagnostic
+    return 1
+
+class Example:
+    @staticmethod
+    def static_method():  # no diagnostic
+        return 1
+
+    def method(self):  # no diagnostic
+        def inner():  # no diagnostic
+            return 1
+        return inner()
+
+    def positional_only(self, /):  # no diagnostic
+        return 1
+
+    def variadic(*args):  # no diagnostic
+        return 1
+
+    @classmethod
+    def class_method(cls):  # no diagnostic
+        return 1
+
+    @classmethod
+    def variadic_class_method(*args):  # no diagnostic
+        return 1
+```
+
+## Keyword-only parameters
+
+Keyword-only parameters cannot receive a positional receiver. For compatibility
+with Pylint's E0211, `**kwargs` is exempt even though it cannot receive one either.
+
+```py
+class Example:
+    def keyword_only(*, self):  # error: [no-method-argument]
+        return 1
+
+    @classmethod
+    def keyword_only_class_method(*, cls):  # error: [no-method-argument]
+        return 1
+
+    def kwargs_only(**kwargs):  # no diagnostic
+        return 1
+
+    def variadic(*args, keyword=None):  # no diagnostic
+        return 1
+```
+
+## Special methods
+
+`__new__` receives the class explicitly from Python's constructor machinery.
+`__init_subclass__` and `__class_getitem__` are implicitly class methods.
+

+    def __new__():  # error: [no-method-argument]
+        return object.__new__(Example)
+
+    def __init__():  # error: [no-method-argument]
+        pass
+
+    def __init_subclass__():  # error: [no-method-argument]
+        pass
+
+    def __class_getitem__():  # error: [no-method-argument]
+        return 1
+
+class Meta(type):
+    def method():  # error: [no-method-argument]
+        return 1
+
+class ExplicitStaticNew:
+    @staticmethod
+    def __new__():  # error: [no-method-argument]
+        return object.__new__(ExplicitStaticNew)
+
+class ExplicitStaticInitSubclass:
+    @staticmethod
+    def __init_subclass__():  # no diagnostic
+        pass
+```
+
+## Intentional class-only calls
+
+A function accessed directly on the class can be called without an instance.
+The rule still flags its definition because calling it through an instance fails.

+        return 1
+

+        return 1
+

+```

+lint.select = ["N804", "N805"]
+```
+
+Selecting naming rules alone does not enable the missing-argument check.

+```py

+        return 1
+
+    @classmethod
+    def class_method():  # no diagnostic
+        return 1
+
+    def wrong_name(this):  # error: [invalid-first-argument-name-for-method]

+
+    @classmethod

+        return 1
+```
+
+## Custom method decorators
+
+```toml

+lint.select = ["PLE0211"]
+lint.pep8-naming.staticmethod-decorators = ["example.static"]
+lint.pep8-naming.classmethod-decorators = ["example.class_method"]
+```

body: With the bitset `ConstraintProvenance`, I'm not convinced this nested-allocation layout makes sense, with up to seven entries for every possible combination of bits. Codex ran some tests and reported that ~90% of upper bounds have 0 or 1 clauses, which strongly favors simplifying this to an `FxOrderSet<(ConstraintProvenance, Type)>` instead -- that keeps hashed deduplication but avoids nested double container allocation. I think that version also simplifies the readers considerably.

Kind of mentioned below, but I'm not sure it makes sense to have a method like this that is used only when there is declared context. Our "choose a compatible specialization" logic should be more generalized than that.

I think we need to rebase this PR on top of (now merged) #28303 in order to better understand how this interacts with the logic in that PR. If that rebase is done naively I think the "choose the first specialization that works" logic here will cause us to lose precision relative to main in cases where #28303 would be able to intersect the multiple alternatives -- but only if there is return context, which is kind of weird. I think the right integration of the two is that we should check the #28303 merged specialization first and use that if it works, then check the merged specialization and use that if it works, and only then go through the single options and pick one?

It's still not really clear to me that it makes sense to use this "pick one" logic specifically only if there is return context. There are also cases where the merged specialization just fails the call entirely (even without return context, because it makes the argument checks fail), and we'd be better off picking one specialization that works. So I think this logic maybe should be applied more broadly than just when there is return context.

This is a bit confusing because "evidence" is no longer part of the bitset. I think it would be clearer here to describe both inferred and declared bounds upfront, and then note that we call both of these evidence bounds.

here's another (slightly different) test that seems redundant assuming no empty provenances, and that maybe deserves its own name (`is_evidence_only` might cover both cases?)

Isn't the `is_evidence` part of this redundant? (I guess not if there can be an empty provenance, but I don't think that can occur?)

Should this whole check (including the "not concrete or doesn't have an unspecialized type var" check below) be given a semantically meaningful name as a method on the constraint?

Should `CandidateTypeVarSolution` hold onto the `inferable` set used to compute its bounds? Then `CandidateSolutions::solve` wouldn't need it again, and `solve_with` callbacks could call `bounds.solve` or `bounds.accepts_candidate` without passing it either. That would also prevent us from accidentally checking a candidate with a different `inferable` set than the one we used to compute it.

`TypeVarSet` is an interned handle, so pretty small, but we would be storing that handle for every type variable on every path. If that noticeably grows the cached results, we could instead store it once on `CandidateSolutions::Constrained`, and give callbacks a borrowed view that pairs the bounds with the set.

Or we could skip the view and have `solve_with` call `choose(variance, bounds, inferable)` with the set from `Constrained`. A callback using the default solver would then look like `|_, bounds, inferable| bounds.solve(db, env, builder, inferable)`. It wouldn't need to capture the set from outside the closure, but it would still have to pass it to `bounds.solve` or `bounds.accepts_candidate`. With the view, the callback could just call `bounds.solve(db, env, builder)` because the view already has the set.
I'm not sure I understand all the operations this does not do, or how this is relevant. IMO, the first part is entirely sufficient.

I think we need to distinguish the declared union from a single member we’re trying speculatively. With an `Any` argument in this example and a declared union type, we now infer the first element of the union we try, rather than inferring the entire union.

```python
from typing import Any

def identity[T](value: T) -> T:
    return value

def f(value: Any) -> None:
    x: int | str = identity(value)
    reveal_type(x)  # now `int`, should be `int | str`
    y: str | int = identity(value)
    reveal_type(y)  # now `str`, should be `str | int`
```

Main (and all other type checkers) infer both `x` and `y` as the declared union in this example. 

For `items: Iterator[Any]`, we also infer `None` for `x: int | None = next(items, None)` and report that `x is None` is always true. [Home Assistant example](https://github.com/home-assistant/core/blob/40881ede942c0135c8ffcc4cb43c807c7177edc1/homeassistant/components/deconz/services.py#L71)

Could we apply the declared-type preference to the full annotation when the argument evidence doesn’t distinguish between its members?

This can let an invalid generic return through even when the list has a concrete element and there’s no `Any` in the program.

```python
def keep[U](values: list[U]) -> list[U]:
    return values

def make[T](arg: T) -> list[T]:
    values = [42]
    return keep(values)

make("x")[0].upper()
```

Main reports `invalid-return-type` on `return keep(values)`. This PR wrongly accepts the program. Enabling `unsound-return-statement` shows that the inferred return is `list[Divergent]`. I guess we are entering recursion when trying to infer the type of `[42]` from uses, but this is a case where we should really just fall back to inferring it as `list[int]`, not as `list[Divergent]`.

This drops the useful part of a partially specialized callback type, so we miss an error here:

```python
from collections.abc import Callable

def identity[T](value: T) -> T:
    return value

def consume[T](callback: Callable[[T, int], int]) -> None:
    pass

consume(identity(lambda x, y: y.upper()))
```

Main reports that `int` has no attribute `upper`; this PR accepts the call. The callback bound contains an unspecialized marker for the first parameter, but its second parameter is still known to be `int`. Dropping the whole bound loses that context and makes `y` unknown. Could we preserve the concrete parts for contextual inference while still preventing provisional markers from escaping into final specializations?

We seem to produce an unsatisfiable call here and fallback to `Unknown`, which allows the call to succeed. This should be a straightforward fix around preserving argument errors after falling back to the recovery specialization. There are a number of limitations around the recovery specialization that lead to similar issues.

This shows up quite a lot in our mdtests after this change, but it is primarily an inconsistency in our narrowing behavior when wrapping a union-returning generic call in a call to `identity`/`reveal_type`, which triggers union narrowing. There's a somewhat related issue involving `TypedDict` narrowing here https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/3935. I don't think this is a very significant problem in practice, but I do plan to look into this issue more generally at some point after this lands.

+//! Computes source edits for Python file renames.\
+//!
+//! ## Overview
+//!
+//! [`will_rename_files`] maps filesystem renames to module names, then plans alias name, module
+//! field, and reference rewrites in the candidate files supplied by the caller (for definitions of
+//! those terms, please see the "Terminology" section below). It does not move files, discover
+//! package contents, validate the filesystem operation, or normalize the returned edits.
+//!
+//! EXAMPLE:
+//!
+//! When `pkg/old.py` is renamed to `pkg/new.py`, the following code:
+//!
+//! ```python
+//! from pkg import old
+//! print(old.C)
+//! ```
+//!
+//! is updated like so:
+//!
+//! ```python
+//! from pkg import new
+//! print(new.C)
+//! ```
+//!
+//! [`will_rename_files`] computes edits over all files in parallel using [`edits_for_file`]. That
+//! in turn computes edits for a single file in two distinct AST passes: [`ImportEditPlanner`]
+//! computes alias name and module field rewrites, then [`ReferenceEditPlanner`] computes reference
+//! rewrites. Those two sets of edits are combined to produce the final result.
+//!
+//! ## Terminology
+//!
+//! Below is the anatomy of the two types of import statement.
+//!
+//! A "plain" import statement:
+//!
+//! ```text
+//!              alias
+//!        +---------------+
+//! import pkg.old as stable
+//!        |          |
+//!        |          alias asname
+//!        alias name
+//! ```
+//!
+//! and an "import from" statement:
+//!
+//! ```text

+use crate::RangedValue;
+use rayon::prelude::*;

+use ty_python_core::ProgramFile;
+use ty_python_core::definition::{Definition, DefinitionKind};
+use ty_python_core::place::PlaceExpr;
+use ty_python_semantic::types::Type;
+use ty_python_semantic::{DefinitionResolution, HasType, SemanticModel};

+/// Computes source edits for a batch of Python file renames.
+///
+/// The following types of rename request are not yet supported:
+///
+/// - A request that renames a directory
+/// - A request that changes a module parent (e.g., renaming `a.old` to `b.new` or `new`)

+/// - A request that changes the extension of a module (e.g., from `.py` to `.pyi`)
+///
+/// When a rename batch contains both supported and unsupported requests, the unsupported requests
+/// are skipped while the supported ones produce edits as normal.
+///
+/// The `files` argument must include every source the caller wants analyzed and the `db` argument
+/// must have place load recording enabled.
+///
+/// The returned edits refer to the original files and source ranges. Unsupported or ambiguous
+/// occurrences are omitted, so a non-empty result does not imply that every reference was updated.
+/// The caller must sort the edits and handle duplicates and overlaps before applying them.
+fn will_rename_files(
+    db: &dyn Db,
+    renames: &[FileRename],
+    files: impl IntoIterator<Item = File>,
+) -> Vec<FileRenameEdit> {
+    let mut files: Vec<_> = files.into_iter().collect();
+    let module_name_changes = ModuleNameChanges::new(db, renames, &files);
+    if module_name_changes.module_renames.is_empty() {
+        return Vec::new();
+    }
+
+    files.sort_unstable_by_key(|file| file.path(db).as_ref());
+    files.dedup();
+
+    files
+        .into_par_iter()
+        .map_with_db(db, |db, file| {
+            edits_for_file(db, file, &module_name_changes)
+        })
+        .flatten()
+        .collect()
+}
+
+/// One Python file rename in a batch.
+struct FileRename {
+    /// The source file before the rename.
+    file: File,
+    /// The destination path, which need not exist yet.
+    new_path: SystemPathBuf,
+}
+
+/// A replacement and the file range containing it.
+type FileRenameEdit = RangedValue<String>;
+
+/// Maps old module names to new module names for supported file renames.
+struct ModuleNameChanges {
+    // A map from old module name to new module name for supported rename operations.
+    module_renames: FxHashMap<ModuleName, ModuleName>,
+    // The module basename for each key in `module_renames`.
+    // This is used to filter out irrelevant files and identifiers to avoid unnecessary semantic analysis.
+    old_module_basenames: FxHashSet<String>,
+    // Files whose imports can contribute bound name changes.
+    candidate_files: FxHashSet<File>,
+}

+impl ModuleNameChanges {
+    fn new(db: &dyn Db, renames: &[FileRename], files: &[File]) -> Self {
+        let module_renames: FxHashMap<_, _> = renames
+            .iter()
+            .filter_map(|rename| module_rename(db, rename))
+            .filter(|(old_module_name, new_module_name)| old_module_name != new_module_name)
+            .collect();

+            .keys()
+            .map(|module_name| module_name.last_component().to_owned())
+            .collect();

+        }
+    }

+    fn new_module_name(&self, old_module_name: &ModuleName) -> Option<&ModuleName> {
+        self.module_renames.get(old_module_name)
+    }
+
+    fn is_old_module_basename(&self, name: &str) -> bool {
+        self.old_module_basenames.contains(name)
+    }
+
+    /// Returns whether the source may need edits for these module name changes.
+    ///
+    /// Source text that doesn't contain any of the old module basenames can
+    /// safely be skipped.
+    ///

+    /// ASCII, because non-ASCII identifiers can normalize to a different
+    /// spelling in the AST.
+    fn may_affect_source(&self, source: &str) -> bool {
+        if !source.is_ascii()
+            || self
+                .old_module_basenames
+                .iter()
+                .any(|basename| !basename.is_ascii())
+        {

+        }

+        self.old_module_basenames
+            .iter()
+            .any(|basename| source.contains(basename))

+}
+
+/// Plans edits for one candidate file in two AST passes.
+///
+/// 1. [`ImportEditPlanner`] plans alias name and module field rewrites and records bound name changes.
+/// 2. [`ReferenceEditPlanner`] plans reference rewrites, including those in string annotations.
+///    Reaching definitions determine which module references need updating after a bound name change.
+///
+/// Planning alias name rewrites first lets us base reference rewrites on the bound name changes,
+/// accounting for alias asnames and re-exports. A rejected alias name rewrite leaves its bound name
+/// unchanged.
+fn edits_for_file(
+    db: &dyn Db,
+    file: File,
+    module_name_changes: &ModuleNameChanges,
+) -> Vec<FileRenameEdit> {

+        return Vec::new();
+    }

+    let model = SemanticModel::new(db, program_file);

+    let mut imports = ImportEditPlanner::new(db, &model, module_name_changes);
+    root.visit_source_order(&mut imports);

+    let mut references = ReferenceEditPlanner::new(
+        db,
+        &model,
+        module_name_changes,
+        &imports.output.bound_name_changes,
+    );
+    root.visit_source_order(&mut references);
+
+    let mut edits = imports.output.edits;
+    edits.extend(references.edits);
+    edits
+}

+/// Computes alias name and module field rewrites, and records bound name changes.
+///
+/// For example, renaming `pkg.old` to `pkg.new` changes

+/// ```python

+/// ```

+///
+/// ```python
+/// import pkg.new
+/// ```

+/// and
+///
+/// ```python
+/// from pkg.old import C
+/// ```

+/// to
+///
+/// ```python
+/// from pkg.new import C
+/// ```

+/// For the moment, the computed edits never change the form of an import statement. For instance,
+/// we never introduce an alias asname where there wasn't one before, or change the import level in
+/// a relative import.
+///
+/// The planner uses [`ReexportAnalyzer`] to follow bound name changes through re-exports.
+struct ImportEditPlanner<'a, 'db> {
+    analyzer: ImportAnalyzer<'a, 'db>,
+    output: ImportAnalysis<'db>,
+}
+
+impl<'a, 'db> ImportEditPlanner<'a, 'db> {
+    fn new(
+        db: &'db dyn Db,
+        model: &'a SemanticModel<'db>,
+        module_name_changes: &'a ModuleNameChanges,
+    ) -> Self {

+        }
+    }

+impl<'a> SourceOrderVisitor<'a> for ImportEditPlanner<'a, '_> {
+    fn enter_node(&mut self, node: AnyNodeRef<'a>) -> TraversalSignal {
+        let output = match node {
+            AnyNodeRef::StmtImport(statement) => self.analyzer.analyze_plain_import(statement),
+            AnyNodeRef::StmtImportFrom(statement) => self
+                .analyzer
+                .analyze_import_from(statement, &mut ReexportAnalyzer::default()),
+            _ => return TraversalSignal::Traverse,
+        };
+
+        if let Some(output) = output {
+            self.output.extend(output);
+        }
+
+        TraversalSignal::Skip
+    }
+
+    // Plain import statements and import from statements cannot occur inside expressions.
+    fn visit_expr(&mut self, _expr: &'a ast::Expr) {}
+}
+
+/// Analyzes one plain import statement or import from statement for [`ImportEditPlanner`].
+struct ImportAnalyzer<'a, 'db> {
+    db: &'db dyn Db,
+    model: &'a SemanticModel<'db>,
+    module_name_changes: &'a ModuleNameChanges,
+}
+
+impl<'a, 'db> ImportAnalyzer<'a, 'db> {
+    fn new(
+        db: &'db dyn Db,
+        model: &'a SemanticModel<'db>,
+        module_name_changes: &'a ModuleNameChanges,
+    ) -> Self {
+        Self {
+            db,
+            model,
+            module_name_changes,
+        }
+    }

+    /// Plans alias name rewrites for a plain import statement, such as `import old` to `import new`.
+    ///
+    /// Returns `None` if no source edits or bound name changes are produced.
+    fn analyze_plain_import(&self, statement: &ast::StmtImport) -> Option<ImportAnalysis<'db>> {
+        let output = self.alias_name_rewrites(&statement.names, |alias| {
+            self.rewrite_plain_import_alias_name(alias)
+        })?;
+
+        (!output.is_empty()).then_some(output)
+    }
+
+    /// Plans alias name and module field rewrites for an import from statement.
+    ///
+    /// For example, `from pkg import old` becomes `from pkg import new`, and
+    /// `from pkg.old import C` becomes `from pkg.new import C`.
+    ///
+    /// Returns `None` when we decline to edit the import statement, or the rename produces no
+    /// source edits or bound name changes.
+    fn analyze_import_from(
+        &self,
+        statement: &ast::StmtImportFrom,
+        reexports: &mut ReexportAnalyzer<'db>,
+    ) -> Option<ImportAnalysis<'db>> {
+        let resolved_module = self.model.resolve_module(
+            statement.module.as_ref().map(ast::Identifier::as_str),
+            statement.level,
+        )?;
+        let module_field_rewrite = if let Some(new_module_name) = self
+            .module_name_changes
+            .new_module_name(resolved_module.name(self.db))
+        {
+            let module = statement.module.as_ref()?;
+            Some(self.module_field_rewrite(module, new_module_name))
+        } else {
+            None
+        };
+
+        let Some(mut output) = self.alias_name_rewrites(&statement.names, |alias| {
+            self.rewrite_import_from_alias_name(alias, resolved_module, reexports)
+        }) else {
+            // Rejecting an alias name rewrite also discards any module field rewrite.
+            return None;
+        };
+
+        if let Some(module_field_rewrite) = module_field_rewrite {
+            output.edits.push(module_field_rewrite);
+        }
+
+        (!output.is_empty()).then_some(output)
+    }
+
+    /// Constructs alias name rewrites and records their bound name changes.
+    ///
+    /// For example, renaming `pkg/old.py` to `pkg/new.py` changes the alias name `pkg.old` in

+    /// changes the alias name `old` in `from pkg import old` to `new` and also changes the bound

+    ///

+    /// of the alias names (e.g., `from facade import old` when `facade` conditionally re-exports
+    /// `pkg.old` or `other.old`, but only `pkg.old` is renamed).
+    fn alias_name_rewrites(
+        &self,
+        aliases: &[ast::Alias],
+        mut rewrite_alias_name: impl FnMut(&ast::Alias) -> RewriteDecision,

body: I've changed this to match other LSP operations; I did it like this originally because I was confused about how we handle unsaved buffers, but now I believe that to be orthogonal.

Yes, but edits are not guaranteed to be complete. The file system rename operation goes forward regardless, so the general philosophy is to make as many correct edits as we can (because regardless the project will be broken until the user takes action, so we might as well get them as far as we can).

I've updated some names to make this clearer, but this does indeed operate in two passes over the AST: the first pass rewrites import statements and stores the bound names that change as a result, and then the second pass rewrites all references to bound names that have changed.

body:
If I understand correctly, you're talking specifically about an unaliased re-export, and you're suggesting that we should not rewrite the import in `facade.py` to `from pkg import new`:

```python
# facade.py
from pkg import old
```

```python
# consumer.py
from facade import old
print(old.value)
```

If that's accurate, then although I think that's a reasonable suggestion, I decided against it because it goes counter to the precedent established by Pylance and basedpyright, both of which rewrite the import in `facade.py` to `from pkg import new`[^1] (and also rewrite both instance of the symbol `old` in `consumer.py` to `new`, as we do also). Conversely, if the re-export were explicitly aliased (e.g., `from pkg import old as old`) then we would preserve that explicit alias (i.e., `from pkg import new as old`).

[^1]: Mypy and pyright do not support file rename; pyrefly's behaviour is incorrect/incomplete in that it doesn't rewrite the import at all.

+use ruff_db::source::source_text;

+/// Computes source edits for a batch of Python file renames.
+///
+/// The following types of rename request are not yet supported:
+///
+/// - A request that renames a directory
+/// - A request that changes a module parent (e.g., renaming `a.old` to `b.new` or `new`)
+/// - A request that renames an `__init__.py` or `__init__.pyi` file
+/// - A request that changes the extension of a module (e.g., from `.py` to `.pyi`)
+///
+/// When a rename batch contains both supported and unsupported requests, the unsupported requests
+/// are skipped while the supported ones produce edits as normal.
+///
+/// The `files` argument must include every source the caller wants analyzed and the `db` argument
+/// must have place load recording enabled.
+///
+/// The returned edits refer to the original files and source ranges. Unsupported or ambiguous
+/// occurrences are omitted, so a non-empty result does not imply that every reference was updated.
+/// The caller must sort the edits and handle duplicates and overlaps before applying them.
+fn will_rename_files(
+    db: &dyn Db,
+    renames: &[FileRename],
+    files: impl IntoIterator<Item = File>,
+) -> Vec<FileRenameEdit> {
+    let mut files: Vec<_> = files.into_iter().collect();
+    let module_name_changes = ModuleNameChanges::new(db, renames, &files);
+    if module_name_changes.module_renames.is_empty() {
+        return Vec::new();
+    }
+
+    files.sort_unstable_by_key(|file| file.path(db).as_ref());
+    files.dedup();
+
+    files
+        .into_par_iter()
+        .map_with_db(db, |db, file| {
+            edits_for_file(db, file, &module_name_changes)
+        })
+        .flatten()
+        .collect()
+}

+/// One Python file rename in a batch.
+struct FileRename {
+    /// The source file before the rename.
+    file: File,
+    /// The destination path, which need not exist yet.
+    new_path: SystemPathBuf,
+}

+type FileRenameEdit = RangedValue<String>;

+/// Maps old module names to new module names for supported file renames.
+struct ModuleNameChanges {
+    // A map from old module name to new module name for supported rename operations.
+    module_renames: FxHashMap<ModuleName, ModuleName>,
+    // The module basename for each key in `module_renames`.
+    // This is used to filter out irrelevant files and identifiers to avoid unnecessary semantic analysis.
+    old_module_basenames: FxHashSet<String>,
+    // Files whose imports can contribute bound name changes.
+    candidate_files: FxHashSet<File>,
+}

+impl ModuleNameChanges {
+    fn new(db: &dyn Db, renames: &[FileRename], files: &[File]) -> Self {
+        let module_renames: FxHashMap<_, _> = renames
+            .iter()
+            .filter_map(|rename| module_rename(db, rename))
+            .filter(|(old_module_name, new_module_name)| old_module_name != new_module_name)
+            .collect();
+        let old_module_basenames = module_renames
+            .keys()
+            .map(|module_name| module_name.last_component().to_owned())
+            .collect();

+            module_renames,
+            old_module_basenames,
+            candidate_files: files.iter().copied().collect(),

+    }

+        self.module_renames.get(old_module_name)

+    fn may_affect_source(&self, source: &str) -> bool {

+                .old_module_basenames
+                .iter()
+                .any(|basename| !basename.is_ascii())

+            .iter()

+/// Plans edits for one candidate file in two AST passes.

+/// 1. [`ImportEditPlanner`] plans alias name and module field rewrites and records bound name changes.
+/// 2. [`ReferenceEditPlanner`] plans reference rewrites, including those in string annotations.
+///    Reaching definitions determine which module references need updating after a bound name change.
+///
+/// Planning alias name rewrites first lets us base reference rewrites on the bound name changes,
+/// accounting for alias asnames and re-exports. A rejected alias name rewrite leaves its bound name
+/// unchanged.
+fn edits_for_file(
+    db: &dyn Db,
+    file: File,
+    module_name_changes: &ModuleNameChanges,
+) -> Vec<FileRenameEdit> {
+    let program_file = db.program_file(file);
+    let source = source_text(db, file);
+    if source.read_error().is_some() {
+        return Vec::new();
+    }
+
+    if !module_name_changes.may_affect_source(source.as_str()) {
+        return Vec::new();
+    }

+    let parsed_module = ruff_db::parsed::parsed_module(db, program_file.python_file(db)).load(db);
+    let root = AnyNodeRef::from(parsed_module.syntax());
+    let model = SemanticModel::new(db, program_file);
+
+    let mut imports = ImportEditPlanner::new(db, &model, module_name_changes);
+    root.visit_source_order(&mut imports);
+
+    let mut references = ReferenceEditPlanner::new(
+        db,
+        &model,
+        module_name_changes,
+        &imports.output.bound_name_changes,
+    );
+    root.visit_source_order(&mut references);
+
+    let mut edits = imports.output.edits;
+    edits.extend(references.edits);

+/// Computes alias name and module field rewrites, and records bound name changes.
+///
+/// For example, renaming `pkg.old` to `pkg.new` changes

+/// ```python
+/// import pkg.old
+/// ```
+///
+/// to
+///
+/// ```python
+/// import pkg.new
+/// ```
+///
+/// and
+///
+/// ```python
+/// from pkg.old import C
+/// ```
+///
+/// to
+///
+/// ```python
+/// from pkg.new import C
+/// ```
+///
+/// For the moment, the computed edits never change the form of an import statement. For instance,
+/// we never introduce an alias asname where there wasn't one before, or change the import level in
+/// a relative import.
+///
+/// The planner uses [`ReexportAnalyzer`] to follow bound name changes through re-exports.
+struct ImportEditPlanner<'a, 'db> {
+    analyzer: ImportAnalyzer<'a, 'db>,
+    output: ImportAnalysis<'db>,
+}
+
+impl<'a, 'db> ImportEditPlanner<'a, 'db> {
+    fn new(
+        db: &'db dyn Db,
+        model: &'a SemanticModel<'db>,
+        module_name_changes: &'a ModuleNameChanges,
+    ) -> Self {
+        Self {
+            analyzer: ImportAnalyzer::new(db, model, module_name_changes),
+            output: ImportAnalysis::default(),
+        }
+    }
+}
+
+impl<'a> SourceOrderVisitor<'a> for ImportEditPlanner<'a, '_> {
+    fn enter_node(&mut self, node: AnyNodeRef<'a>) -> TraversalSignal {
+        let output = match node {
+            AnyNodeRef::StmtImport(statement) => self.analyzer.analyze_plain_import(statement),
+            AnyNodeRef::StmtImportFrom(statement) => self
+                .analyzer
+                .analyze_import_from(statement, &mut ReexportAnalyzer::default()),
+            _ => return TraversalSignal::Traverse,
+        };
+
+        if let Some(output) = output {
+            self.output.extend(output);
+        }
+
+        TraversalSignal::Skip
+    }
+
+    // Plain import statements and import from statements cannot occur inside expressions.
+    fn visit_expr(&mut self, _expr: &'a ast::Expr) {}
+}
+
+/// Analyzes one plain import statement or import from statement for [`ImportEditPlanner`].
+struct ImportAnalyzer<'a, 'db> {
+    db: &'db dyn Db,
+    model: &'a SemanticModel<'db>,
+    module_name_changes: &'a ModuleNameChanges,
+}
+
+impl<'a, 'db> ImportAnalyzer<'a, 'db> {
+    fn new(
+        db: &'db dyn Db,
+        model: &'a SemanticModel<'db>,
+        module_name_changes: &'a ModuleNameChanges,
+    ) -> Self {
+        Self {
+            db,
+            model,
+            module_name_changes,
+        }
+    }
+
+    /// Plans alias name rewrites for a plain import statement, such as `import old` to `import new`.
+    ///
+    /// Returns `None` if no source edits or bound name changes are produced.
+    fn analyze_plain_import(&self, statement: &ast::StmtImport) -> Option<ImportAnalysis<'db>> {
+        let output = self.alias_name_rewrites(&statement.names, |alias| {
+            self.rewrite_plain_import_alias_name(alias)
+        })?;
+
+        (!output.is_empty()).then_some(output)
+    }
+
+    /// Plans alias name and module field rewrites for an import from statement.
+    ///
+    /// For example, `from pkg import old` becomes `from pkg import new`, and
+    /// `from pkg.old import C` becomes `from pkg.new import C`.
+    ///
+    /// Returns `None` when we decline to edit the import statement, or the rename produces no
+    /// source edits or bound name changes.
+    fn analyze_import_from(
+        &self,
+        statement: &ast::StmtImportFrom,
+        reexports: &mut ReexportAnalyzer<'db>,
+    ) -> Option<ImportAnalysis<'db>> {
+        let resolved_module = self.model.resolve_module(
+            statement.module.as_ref().map(ast::Identifier::as_str),
+            statement.level,
+        )?;
+        let module_field_rewrite = if let Some(new_module_name) = self
+            .module_name_changes
+            .new_module_name(resolved_module.name(self.db))
+        {
+            let module = statement.module.as_ref()?;
+            Some(self.module_field_rewrite(module, new_module_name))
+        } else {
+            None
+        };
+
+        let Some(mut output) = self.alias_name_rewrites(&statement.names, |alias| {
+            self.rewrite_import_from_alias_name(alias, resolved_module, reexports)
+        }) else {
+            // Rejecting an alias name rewrite also discards any module field rewrite.
+            return None;
+        };
+
+        if let Some(module_field_rewrite) = module_field_rewrite {
+            output.edits.push(module_field_rewrite);
+        }
+
+        (!output.is_empty()).then_some(output)
+    }
+
+    /// Constructs alias name rewrites and records their bound name changes.
+    ///
+    /// For example, renaming `pkg/old.py` to `pkg/new.py` changes the alias name `pkg.old` in
+    /// `import pkg.old` to `pkg.new`, but keeps the bound name `pkg`. Conversely, the same rename
+    /// changes the alias name `old` in `from pkg import old` to `new` and also changes the bound
+    /// name.
+    ///
+    /// Returns `None` when we decline to rewrite the import statement because we can't rewrite one
+    /// of the alias names (e.g., `from facade import old` when `facade` conditionally re-exports
+    /// `pkg.old` or `other.old`, but only `pkg.old` is renamed).
+    fn alias_name_rewrites(
+        &self,
+        aliases: &[ast::Alias],
+        mut rewrite_alias_name: impl FnMut(&ast::Alias) -> RewriteDecision,
+    ) -> Option<ImportAnalysis<'db>> {
+        let mut output = ImportAnalysis::default();
+
+        for alias in aliases {
+            let new_alias_name = match rewrite_alias_name(alias) {
+                RewriteDecision::Preserve => continue,
+                RewriteDecision::Replace(new_alias_name) => new_alias_name,
+                RewriteDecision::Omit => return None,
+            };
+
+            if alias.asname.is_none() {
+                // Without an alias asname, a plain import statement such as `import pkg.old`
+                // binds `pkg`, while an import from statement such as `from pkg import old`
+                // binds `old`. Therefore, we can compute the old bound name in both cases
+                // by retrieving just the first component.
+                let old_bound_name = Self::first_component(alias.name.as_str());
+
+                // The replacement alias name obeys the same rule: `pkg.new` binds `pkg`,
+                // while `new` binds `new`. Retrieve its first component for the new bound name.
+                let new_bound_name = Self::first_component(&new_alias_name);
+
+                if old_bound_name != new_bound_name {
+                    let definition =
+                        ty_python_core::semantic_index(self.db, self.model.program_file())
+                            .expect_single_definition(alias);
+                    output
+                        .bound_name_changes
+                        .insert(definition, new_bound_name.to_owned());
+                }
+            }
+
+            output
+                .edits
+                .push(self.source_edit(alias.name.range, new_alias_name));
+        }
+
+        // An empty alias analysis is valid: an import from statement may still have a
+        // module field rewrite. The caller checks the combined analysis for emptiness.
+        Some(output)
+    }

+    /// in the statement `import pkg.old`).
+    fn rewrite_plain_import_alias_name(&self, alias: &ast::Alias) -> RewriteDecision {
+        let Some(resolved_module) = self.model.resolve_module(Some(alias.name.as_str()), 0) else {
+            return RewriteDecision::Preserve;
+        };
+
+        let Some(new_module_name) = self
+            .module_name_changes
+            .new_module_name(resolved_module.name(self.db))
+        else {
+            return RewriteDecision::Preserve;
+        };

+        RewriteDecision::replace_if_changed(alias.name.as_str(), new_module_name.as_str())
+    }

+    /// Chooses an alias name rewrite for an import from statement, including re-exports.

+    fn rewrite_import_from_alias_name(
+        &self,
+        alias: &ast::Alias,
+        resolved_module: Module<'db>,
+        reexports: &mut ReexportAnalyzer<'db>,
+    ) -> RewriteDecision {
